findings: The analyzer groups event_id // 1000000, treats the quotient as boot time and extends the interval to the last first_seen_at in that group. Its comment calls this verified uptime.

Historical IdGenerator resumes current at persisted reserved_through after restart, reserves another batch, then issues incremented integers. Only cold seeding uses a wall-clock floor, and recovery can instead select a larger historical ID. Therefore the quotient is not a guaranteed boot identity or timestamp.
A restart can preserve the quotient, and a long-lived process can cross a million-ID boundary. A common quotient proves neither one process lifetime nor uninterrupted host availability.

The load_wake_boots docstring describes limiting observed uptime to two hours after a signal, but the implementation only computes signal indices and appends the full interval; it does not apply that limit.
The progress loader accepts matching Bash invocation text without checking command success. The recorded progress model is therefore not uniformly durable output.

arithmetic_counterexample.qualification: Arithmetic application of the inspected load/next rules, not an executed runtime or observed restart.

omitted_run_interpretation: All three already occur in analysis_meta.json as khala runlog spans. Their absence from the presentation table is not evidence they were excluded from denominator construction.
limits: This source revision is historical code evidence, not an attestation of every loaded daemon build.
No reconstructed corrected uptime denominator or replacement gap percentage is claimed.
Retained interval arithmetic still reproduces; the uptime interpretation does not follow from the event-ID contract.
Host suspension, missing log intervals and complete progress coverage require separate evidence.
